title: Going Green for Less Green: Optimizing the Cost of Reducing Cloud Carbon Emissions
problem: Cloud batch workloads cause high carbon emissions. Temporal shifting of workloads to low-carbon periods reduces emissions but increases job completion times and decreases cost savings from reserved instances due to changed demand patterns leaving resources idle.
motivation: Reducing cloud datacenter carbon emissions is essential as capacity grows exponentially, but must be balanced against performance and cost constraints.
method: GAIA is a scheduler that decides when to run batch computing jobs based on when the electrical grid is cleanest—that is, when it relies most on renewable energy and has lowest carbon intensity. Running jobs immediately is fast but uses dirtier power; delaying them to clean periods reduces emissions but makes jobs take longer and wastes reserved instances (servers you've prepaid for that now sit idle). The scheduler explicitly weighs all three concerns—carbon, speed, and cost—to pick the best timing for each job.
key_novelty: A batch scheduler that explicitly balances carbon emissions, job speed, and infrastructure costs when deciding when to run cloud workloads.
contributions: Quantifies the carbon-performance-cost trade-off in cloud platforms
Proposes scheduling policies that double carbon savings per percentage increase in cost versus existing approaches
Reduces performance overhead by 26% compared to baseline carbon-aware policies
Demonstrates cost-awareness in carbon optimization through demand pattern management

metrics.other: 2x carbon savings per percentage cost increase; 26% reduction in performance overhead

primary_theme: Carbon-aware batch scheduling with cost-performance optimization
